t: #4022 K-th Digit in Infinite String — O(1) Block Arithmetic
o: The string is built from blocks: block 0 is "123456789" (nine 1-digit numbers); every later block holds the ten 2-digit numbers 10b..10b+9, written ascending for even b and descending for odd b, so each later block is exactly 20 digits. Thus after the first 9 digits the structure is perfectly periodic with period 20, letting us jump straight to the block and position containing digit k. For k = 15: drop 9, position 6 lands in the first 2-digit block (odd → "191817161514131211"), 6th digit is '7'.
k: Block 0 contributes 9 digits; every subsequent block contributes exactly 20.
Within a block, the number index is pos/2 and the digit is the tens digit if pos is even, otherwise the ones digit.
Direction alternates with block parity, flipping the number index.

a.i: Strip the 9 digits of block 0; the remainder t = k − 9 indexes into an endless sequence of 20-digit blocks. Block index b = (t−1)/20 corresponds to original block b+1; position pos = (t−1) mod 20 picks number idx = pos/2 within it. If the block number is odd the numbers descend (value 10b′+9−idx), otherwise ascend (10b′+idx). Extract the tens or ones digit according to pos parity.
s: Let t = k − 9; compute b = (t−1) // 20 and pos = (t−1) % 20.
Let blk = b + 1 and idx = pos // 2; number = 10*blk + idx if blk is even else 10*blk + 9 − idx.
Return the tens digit of the number if pos is even, else the ones digit.
a.t: O(1) — a handful of arithmetic operations regardless of k.

w: Verify against all three examples by hand before coding — off-by-one errors at the block-0 boundary and the descending-direction index are the classic mistakes. Note k can be 10¹⁵: 64-bit integers are mandatory in Java/C++ (JS doubles are safe since 10¹⁵ < 2⁵³). Follow-ups: change block size, use 3-digit blocks, or ask for the digit at k in a string built from squares instead of integers.
